text: Last lesson we fed the whole dataset into the model every iteration. Real datasets don't fit that pattern — they're too big, they need shuffling, and training works better in small batches. PyTorch splits this into Dataset, which fetches one example, and DataLoader, which batches and shuffles.

A Dataset only answers two questions: how many examples are there, via len, and how do I get example i, via getitem. That's the hook where you'd load an image from disk or tokenize text, rather than holding everything in memory at once.

DataLoader wraps a Dataset and handles the rest. Iterating over it yields batches, not single examples — each batch stacks batch_size examples along a new leading dimension. This is also the point where an epoch stops meaning one single pass over all your tensors at once, and starts meaning many smaller iterations instead.

Three settings you'll tune constantly. batch_size trades smoother gradients against memory, and picking one is often just a matter of the largest size that still fits comfortably in memory. shuffle should be true for training so the model doesn't learn a biased order, and usually false for validation. num_workers loads the next batch in the background while the GPU is busy with the current one.

If your data already lives in plain tensors, skip writing a custom class entirely — TensorDataset wraps any number of equal-length tensors and indexes them together. It's a convenient shortcut that covers a surprising number of real training setups, especially early on while you're still experimenting.

Swap the from-scratch loop's manual data handling for a real DataLoader, and the five-step training loop from last lesson doesn't change at all. Up next, lesson six: saving and loading a trained model so you don't lose your work.
